newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICAN DEBT OUTLOOK - CAPITAL FLOWS SUPPORT CETES.
newsitem.headline: MEXICAN DEBT OUTLOOK - CAPITAL FLOWS SUPPORT CETES.

text.p: Expectations that capital will keep flooding into Mexico and hold the peso rock-steady make longer-term Mexican treasury bills a good bet, debt analysts said on Wednesday.
"Our recommendation is to buy longer-term Cetes, the six month or 12 month paper," said ING Barings global fixed-income strategist Raul Elizalde.
"The Mexican peso is expected to remain relatively strong and there is a lot of liquidity coming into the local market," he added.
Mexico's stock exchange is setting new record highs on a regular basis, and the flow of funds into the bolsa, and into other instruments, is helping underpin peso strength.
A peso that has defied all expectations of short-term depreciation has quelled fears of a hit from the currency side.
Coupled with real returns of 10.5 percent on 12-month paper, longer-term Mexican paper is "very attractive," Elizalde said.
Moreover, analysts see no near-term end to the capital inflows.
"With continued strength of exports and investment, real interest rates should decline gradually," said Jose Maria Barrionuevo, head of strategy and research for emerging markets at Lehman Brothers.
"Accordingly, one-year Cetes offer the most value in the Cetes curve," he said.
Lehman Brothers noted that local market participants have not taken advantage of the one-year Cetes, partially due to a mismatch between short-term borrowing and a taking of longer-term positions.
As well, concerns over economic policy implications of the make-up of the new Congress appear to have stopped investors from focusing on the longer-term securities.
Still, Merrill Lynch said recently that investments in Mexican Cetes remain their top local currency recommendation.
"We expect annualized U.S. dollar returns for investing in Cetes of 10 percent to 13 percent over the next year," Merrill Lynch's emerging market group said.

The rate on the 28-day Cetes rose 65 basis points to 18.35 percent at Banco de Mexico's primary auction on Tuesday, but the increase was mainly due to technical issues and the downward trend is expected to continue.
Those declines, however, have a floor.
"I don't think that they have much more room (to fall)," Santander Investment economist Hector Chavez told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
He said that inflation over the next six months would be in line with seasonal highs.

"Normally rates rebound a little bit towards the end of the year, so I would say 17.0 percent is the floor for the short-term, for the next six months. And maybe when we see inflation coming down later on in the beginning of 1998, we can expect lower rates," Chavez said.
Positions in Cetes have been lucrative, though.
Mexico was the best performer in J.P. Morgan's Emerging Local Markets Index in July, posting a 3.66 percent increase due to the continued improvement in its fundamentals, the company said.
